title: Generative AI Technologies and Educational Outcomes: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Comparing Traditional and AI-Driven Approaches
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether generative AI (GenAI) tools improve educational outcomes compared with traditional or non-GenAI approaches. It focuses on pooled effects for academic achievement, higher-order thinking, writing skills, GenAI-generated feedback, game-assisted GenAI, country-level differences, and educational-level differences. The authors frame the study as filling a gap in prior reviews, which had focused more narrowly on ChatGPT writing instruction, policy, ethics, or guidelines rather than synthesizing GenAI effects across multiple educational outcomes.

The study uses a PRISMA-based systematic review and meta-analysis. Searches were conducted in Web of Science, Scopus, Springer, Wiley, and ScienceDirect, plus gray literature, yielding 1,096 initial records and 53 included studies after screening. Included interventions covered GenAI technologies such as ChatGPT and other AI-generated content tools, GenAI feedback systems, and game-assisted GenAI. Comparisons included non-GenAI instruction, non-GenAI feedback, and non-game-assisted GenAI conditions.

The included evidence spans educational contexts involving students, teachers, and educational institutions, with subgroup analyses for university and secondary education and for countries including China, Pakistan, Korea, and Turkey. Populations represented in the included studies include high school students, undergraduate and graduate students, and educators/adult participants.

The meta-analysis concludes that GenAI-assisted education generally outperforms non-GenAI approaches for academic achievement, higher-order thinking, learning motivation, and writing skills. GenAI feedback showed a large positive effect relative to non-GenAI feedback, while game-assisted GenAI did not show a statistically significant advantage. Country subgroup results were positive in China and Pakistan but not significant in Korea or Turkey. GenAI effects were significant at both university and secondary levels.
study_country: Multiple countries (including China, Pakistan, Korea, and Turkey)

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI technologies, including large language models and AI chatbots, used in education to generate content, provide feedback, support learning tasks, and assist instruction; the paper synthesizes heterogeneous GenAI tools rather than reporting pooled effects for a single named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper conducted a meta-analysis comparing GenAI-assisted education, GenAI feedback, and game-assisted GenAI with non-GenAI or non-game-assisted approaches across educational outcomes, countries, and educational levels.

findings.finding_summary: Across included studies, GenAI-assisted education caused significantly higher academic achievements than non-GenAI-assisted educational approaches. The pooled effect was small-to-moderate (g=0.40; 95%CI=0.08~0.71); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

GenAI-assisted education caused significantly higher higher-order thinking abilities than non-GenAI-assisted educational approaches. The pooled effect was moderate-to-large (g=0.72; 95%CI=0.30~1.13); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

GenAI-assisted education caused significantly higher learning motivation than non-GenAI-assisted educational approaches. The pooled effect was large (g=0.81; 95%CI=0.20~1.41); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

GenAI-assisted education caused significantly higher writing skills than non-GenAI-assisted educational approaches. The pooled effect was moderate-to-large (g=0.76; 95%CI=0.18~1.35); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

GenAI feedback exerted a significant positive influence on educational outcomes compared with non-GenAI feedback. The pooled effect was large (g=1.27; 95%CI=0.49~2.05); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.
findings.measure: educational outcomes from GenAI feedback versus non-GenAI feedback

findings.finding_summary: Game-assisted GenAI did not cause significant differences in educational outcomes compared with non-game-assisted GenAI. The pooled effect was g=0.24 with a confidence interval crossing zero (95%CI=-0.40~0.88); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.
findings.measure: educational outcomes from game-assisted GenAI versus non-game-assisted GenAI

findings.finding_summary: In the China subgroup, GenAI technologies caused significantly higher educational outcomes than non-GenAI technologies. The pooled effect was g=0.71 with 95%CI=0.5~0.92; participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

In the Pakistan subgroup, GenAI technologies caused significantly higher educational outcomes than non-GenAI technologies. The pooled effect was g=0.75 with 95%CI=0.58~0.92; participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

In the Korea subgroup, no significant difference was found in the effect of GenAI technologies on educational outcomes compared with non-GenAI technologies. The pooled estimate was g=1.68, but the confidence interval crossed zero (95%CI=-0.41~3.78); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

In the Turkey subgroup, no significant difference was found in the effect of GenAI technologies on educational outcomes compared with non-GenAI technologies. The pooled estimate was near zero (g=0.01; 95%CI=-0.23~0.25); participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

At the university level, GenAI technologies caused significantly higher educational outcomes than non-GenAI technologies. The pooled effect was g=.70 with 95%CI=0.52~0.88; participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

At the secondary level, GenAI technologies caused significantly higher educational outcomes than non-GenAI technologies. The pooled effect was g=.80 with 95%CI=0.15~1.44; participant sample sizes were not reported in the provided text.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a PRISMA-based systematic review and meta-analysis including 53 studies, with database search, inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality appraisal, heterogeneity testing, random-effects models, sensitivity analysis, and publication-bias procedures described. Significant heterogeneity and some low-quality included studies are noted, but the design is still a quantitative meta-analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported pooled effects for GenAI were generally medium to large and positive, including academic achievement (g=0.40), higher-order thinking (g=0.72), writing skills (g=0.76), GenAI feedback (g=1.27), and university/secondary outcomes (g=0.70/0.80). One subgroup, game-assisted GenAI, was not statistically significant (g=0.24; 95% CI=-0.40~0.88), but the overall impact pattern was positive with effect sizes above 0.20.
